storylines.label: Inference Engines
storylines.latest_title: Can agents write inference engines from scratch in 12 hours and beat vLLM?

editorial.tldr: This is a loose theme thread, not one event: three unrelated sources over two weeks treated the inference engine itself as the object of work. It opened with EngineAgent, a paper on using agents to port new LLM architectures into on-device engines, and a Nov 22 paper on stripping backdoor activations at inference time.
editorial.whats_new: Humanity's Last System (HLS), an open benchmark, gives coding agents live GPU sandboxes for up to 36 hours to build inference servers that are verified and scored for speed against vLLM-style baselines.
editorial.why_it_matters: Agent-written serving code is moving from research prototype to scored benchmark, so the speed claims around custom inference engines will soon come with a public yardstick against vLLM.
editorial.take_for_builders: Treat agent-built inference servers as unproven until HLS publishes verified scores; keep vLLM as the serving baseline and rerun your own latency evals before swapping engines.

storylines.label: Vllm Inference
storylines.latest_title: Can agents write inference engines from scratch in 12 hours and beat vLLM?

editorial.tldr: This is a theme thread, not one event: three separate items treat vLLM as the default open serving stack. It opened with Warmctl, a Show HN tool for faster vLLM cold starts, then vLLM shipped day-0 support for Baidu's ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview through a plugin.
editorial.whats_new: Humanity's Last System (HLS), an open benchmark, gives coding agents live GPU sandboxes for up to 36 hours to build inference servers, then verifies them and scores their speed against vLLM-style baselines.
editorial.why_it_matters: vLLM is now the reference point for serving: new models ship as vLLM plugins, tools patch its cold starts, and agent benchmarks measure themselves against it.
editorial.take_for_builders: For ERNIE 5.5 Flash, pin vllm==0.32.0 with the vllm-ERNIE plugin. Treat HLS results as research until verified scores beat your own vLLM baseline on your models.

storylines.label: Weight-Space Programming
storylines.latest_title: Looped Weight-Space Programming: use AI to set model weights

editorial.tldr: An MIT report that a frontier LLM can write and read small neural network weights in a single reply set off a run of follow-ups in mid-November: an open-source instruction set (W-ISA), a game-agent compilation paper, and an independent replication. A Nov 18 paper then moved from capability edits to value edits, and a Nov 23 CLIP paper borrowed the name for a closed-form weight-editing recipe.
editorial.whats_new: MBZUAI researchers report Claude Opus 5.5 solved only 26% of hard mazes directly, but a transformer it wrote by setting weights solved 100% of their test mazes in 39 minutes for $19, with no training run.
editorial.why_it_matters: If an LLM can hand-author a small model that beats its own direct answers, weight-writing becomes a cheap way to build narrow task solvers, and an untracked way to change a model's behavior.
editorial.take_for_builders: Treat LLM-written weights as a research option for narrow, verifiable tasks only. Add checkpoint hashing and behavior regression evals now, since direct weight edits leave no training trail.

storylines.label: Product OpenAI
storylines.latest_title: QCon San Francisco 2026: Lessons from Building a $100M Product in Six Weeks at OpenAI

editorial.tldr: This is a theme thread, not one event: three accounts of teams shipping product work with OpenAI models and Codex agents. It opened with two OpenAI customer stories, Merge using GPT-6 Astra and Codex for code review and Amplitude's Wave agent driving 1-2 day product changes.
editorial.whats_new: At QCon SF, OpenAI's Brian Yang said the ChatGPT ads product was built with Codex agents and no human-written code, held together by layered testing, sandboxes, and batched PR reviews.
editorial.why_it_matters: The first engineering account in the thread names the controls behind agent-written code (layered tests, sandboxes, batched review), where the customer stories only named the tools.
editorial.take_for_builders: Before letting coding agents merge unattended, put a sandboxed run and a layered test gate in front of every agent PR, and batch reviews rather than skipping them.

storylines.label: GLM-5.4 Loop
storylines.latest_title: Zhipu launches GLM-5.4: 750B base model delivers 2-3T-class performance, Loop architecture debuts in a flagship model

editorial.tldr: Z.ai (Zhipu) released GLM-5.4 on Nov 23, a 750B loop transformer that passes its 28 weight-shared layers twice instead of stacking more unique layers. It is the lab's first looped flagship, pitched at generalized coding, and launched without open weights.
editorial.whats_new: Zhipu now claims the 750B GLM-5.4 matches 2-3T-class models, but that claim comes from Chinese financial press and has no independent benchmark behind it yet.
editorial.why_it_matters: Looping shared layers trades parameter count for repeated compute per token, so GLM-5.4's memory footprint and its latency and cost per token may not scale the way a plain 750B model's would.
editorial.take_for_builders: Do not swap GLM-5.4 into a coding-agent stack on the 2-3T claim; wait for weights or API pricing, then rerun your own coding evals and measure latency per token.

status.detail: The model is announced and described, but open weights and independent evaluations are both still missing.

storylines.label: Efficient Inference
storylines.latest_title: Announcing vLLM-GR: Efficient Inference for Generative Recommendation

editorial.tldr: This is a loose theme thread, not one event: 22 independent items from Nov 6 to Nov 24 that each cut inference or agent cost at a different layer, mostly arXiv papers plus posts from Google, Baseten, Microsoft Research, UW, AWS and vLLM. Through Nov 19 the KV cache was the most-attacked target, ending with RoCoKV and TideCache.
editorial.whats_new: vLLM shipped vLLM-GR on Nov 24, an open-source serving framework that adds beam search over semantic item IDs so generative recommendation models such as OneRec can run on the vLLM stack.
editorial.why_it_matters: KV-cache memory is still the most-attacked bottleneck here (6 of 22 items), and vLLM-GR shows mainstream serving engines now stretching to non-chat workloads, so one serving stack may soon cover both LLM and recommendation traffic.
editorial.take_for_builders: If long-context or reasoning workloads are memory-bound, profile KV-cache size per request before buying GPUs; if you run generative recommendation on a separate stack, test vLLM-GR before building custom beam-search serving.

storylines.label: Benchmarking Multi-Agent
storylines.latest_title: Seeking in Space: Benchmarking Purposeful Active Exploration of Vision-Language Models for Spatial Reasoning

editorial.tldr: This is a theme thread, not one event: three weeks of arXiv papers proposing new agent benchmarks, starting with multi-agent decision and coordination tests (TandemBench, WorkflowArena). Later papers moved to MCP hallucination, memory poisoning, and long-horizon real-world tasks such as AI infra tuning and research sessions.
editorial.whats_new: REPA (Nov 23) models how one agent's local errors propagate into system-level failures across multi-agent workflows, two days after MASSys showed Star vs Chain topology rankings flip under KV-cache pressure.
editorial.why_it_matters: Multi-agent scores now depend on serving substrate and error propagation, not just the model, so a leaderboard number may not hold on your own inference stack.
editorial.take_for_builders: Before choosing a multi-agent topology from a published score, rerun the comparison on your own serving stack at production load, because MASSys shows the ranking can flip with KV-cache pressure.

storylines.label: Spatial Reasoning
storylines.latest_title: Seeking in Space: Benchmarking Purposeful Active Exploration of Vision-Language Models for Spatial Reasoning

editorial.tldr: Three arXiv papers in four days attack the same weakness: vision-language models that misjudge depth, distance, and layout. They share a theme rather than one event, starting with StereoVLM, which feeds calibrated stereo image pairs to a VLM for metric 3D reasoning.
editorial.whats_new: ActSpace-Bench tests whether VLMs explore a scene before answering 994 spatial questions; the strongest models explore purposefully but lose gathered evidence to limited memory.
editorial.why_it_matters: For agents that act on camera input, the papers point at three levers outside the base model: richer sensor input, extra vision encoders, and memory across exploration steps.
editorial.take_for_builders: If an agent answers spatial questions from images, log what it saw at each step and check whether the final answer uses it; ActSpace-Bench points at memory, not perception, as the failure point.

storylines.label: Large Language
storylines.latest_title: ToolSmith: An Automatic Tool-Generation Framework for Multimodal Search Agents

editorial.tldr: This thread is a reading list of LLM research papers grouped by shared wording, not one event. From Nov 4 it ran through agent benchmarks, kernel and serving work, eval validity and multimodal hallucination, then Nov 13-19 papers on abstention, jailbreak screening and lie probes.
editorial.whats_new: Nov 23: ToolSmith has multimodal search agents generate and reuse their own tools across 13 benchmarks, three days after Search-RSI reported 9.8- and 9.5-point gains at 9B and 27B by growing the agent's search world.
editorial.why_it_matters: Most items are single unreplicated preprints, but the late-November run moves toward agents that extend their own tools, search space and memory, which touches tool registries and KV-cache budgets in a serving stack.
editorial.take_for_builders: Before letting an agent add tools or memory at runtime, gate it: review generated tools before they enter the shared registry, log which ones get reused, and measure any cached-memory scheme's answer quality on your own long-context traffic, not only its prefill latency.

storylines.label: Reinforcement Learning
storylines.latest_title: CO-GRAFT: Attributing Reinforcement Learning Gains in Search Agents via Role-Level Policy Grafting

editorial.tldr: This is a theme thread of mostly arXiv papers, not one developing story. Since Nov 4 it has tracked RL for agents: multi-turn and multi-agent training, RL-learned memory, rollout cost, and the finding that RL tool-use gains can raise tool hallucination.
editorial.whats_new: Nov 23: CO-GRAFT finds query generation explains at most 15% of RL gains in Search-R1 agents, and a state-verified RL paper lifts a 27B tutoring agent from 51.47% to 80.74% strict success.
editorial.why_it_matters: If you post-train or operate tool-using agents, this cluster names where RL pays off and what it costs: rollout throughput, tool hallucination, and which agent role actually improved, though nearly every result is author-reported.
editorial.take_for_builders: When evaluating an RL-tuned agent, score tool-hallucination rate and per-role behavior (query, read, answer) next to task success, since the headline gain can hide regressions or come from one role.

storylines.label: Policy Learning
storylines.latest_title: CO-GRAFT: Attributing Reinforcement Learning Gains in Search Agents via Role-Level Policy Grafting

editorial.tldr: This is a theme thread, not one event: six November items share the words "policy learning" or "policy improvement" across speech translation, multi-agent orchestration, robotics, and continual RL. Google's Gemini 4 Argon, framed partly around robot policy improvement, is the only product release in the set.
editorial.whats_new: CO-GRAFT (Nov 23) swaps RL-trained and pre-RL policies role by role in Search-R1 agents and finds query generation accounts for at most 15% of the RL gain.
editorial.why_it_matters: For agent builders, the useful strand is attribution: knowing which agent role RL actually improved tells you where to spend fine-tuning and eval effort.
editorial.take_for_builders: Before RL-tuning a whole search agent, ablate per role (query writing, reading, answering) to find which step the training actually improves.

storylines.label: Prompt Injection
storylines.latest_title: FATCAT: Fault Injection Attacks Targeting Chip-level Alignment

editorial.tldr: This is a topic cluster, not one event: early-November papers proposed a runtime defense for tool-using agents and widened injection testing to task tampering and injected reasoning. A Nov 8 paper argued for treating the model as untrusted, and practitioner posts followed with a lawyerspeak guardrail bypass and a case for authorization scoping.
editorial.whats_new: A Nov 23 paper, Conartist, reports adaptive multi-step injection succeeding 32.12% of the time on a 576-instance tool-use benchmark and 66.67% on a Reddit GUI benchmark across five backbone models.
editorial.why_it_matters: Adaptive, multi-step attacks against computer-using agents land often enough that a text-reading guardrail cannot be the last line; the control that holds is the permission boundary enforced in code around each tool call.
editorial.take_for_builders: Give each agent task the narrowest credentials it needs and gate high-impact tool calls with deterministic policy or human approval, then add adaptive multi-step, task-tampering, and legal-register cases to your red-team suite.
